abstract: Measurement and feedforward let quantum circuits entangle arbitrarily distant qubits in constant depth if measurement records are perfect and classical communication is instantaneous. We allow each reported bit to flip independently with a fixed probability between zero and one half, keeping all gates ideal. Consider a square-lattice device with a unique path between the endpoints and a bounded number of qubits per site. Beyond $\exp[O(D^3)]$ steps along that path, every depth-$D$ circuit starting from a product state leaves the endpoints exactly separable in every record, however rare. By copying outcomes onto spare qubits beside the path before readout, we attain a reach of $\exp[Θ(D^3)]$ for a nondestructive parity measurement at fixed accuracy without postselection. On a one-dimensional chain, the optimal reach for the same measurement is $\exp[Θ(D^2)]$. On any interaction graph, a constant-depth circuit starting from a product state needs $Ω(L\ln L)$ qubits to entangle endpoints at graph distance $L$. The reliability of local readout thus limits the depth advantage of adaptive circuits for long-range entanglement.
